[The Acalābhisamaya of Vanaratna] Tōh. 1783 — Acalābhisamayahṛṣṭābhidhāna (The Joyful Expression of the Realization of Acala)
In the language of India:

*Acālābhisamaya-suratābhidyāna*. In the language of Tibet: *Mi g-yo ba’i mngon par rtogs pa rab tu dga’ bar mdor brjod pa* (The Concise Expression of the Joyful Realization of Acala). Translated by Gzhon nu dpal. Totaling eight folios, recto and verso.
Homage to the glorious, fierce, and wrathful one!
Having prostrated to the assembly of glorious, powerful heroes,
From one's own mental continuum and from seeing other treatises,
Most likely the *Vajrasattvasādhana* of Candrakīrti, titled *The Sādhana of the Glorious Great Wrathful One*.
Extracted from those [works], this shall now be written here.

First of all, the mantrin, desiring to directly realize these very three bodies of all the Buddhas, having trained in the authentic *pāramitās*, having pleased the Vajra Guru, entered the mandala and received empowerment; having been granted the authentic authorization and heard the tantras, he is skilled in the reality of the union (*yuganaddha*).

One who possesses great compassion and, with a mind striving for the benefit of all sentient beings, desires to meditate on the glorious *Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa*, should sit upon a comfortable seat in a place that is agreeable to the mind and free from all harm; or else, "seat" refers to sitting here [upon] a vajra or a mandala of excrement—the body of the most excellent one.
Having sat there, he then placed [the disciple] within a pill of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).

[He taught him] joy (*muditā*), characterized by the complete satisfaction of being inseparable from supreme bliss; and equanimity (*upekṣā*), which delights in bringing forth the path that serves as the antidote to the eight worldly dharmas.

One should cultivate the four abodes of Brahmā. Among them, great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the aspect of establishing happiness through affection for all sentient beings as if they were one's only child. Great compassion (*karuṇā*) is the nature of wishing to deliver all helpless sentient beings, who are submerged in the ocean of conceptual construction, from suffering and the causes of suffering.

From the instruction on the *sādhana* of the most exceptionally sublime immovability (*aniñja*), "joy" is characterized by being completely satisfied through possessing both common and supreme bliss. "Equanimity" is the mode of practicing the path as the antidote to the eight worldly concerns.

Then the yogi, whose nature is immovable, appearing with the color, form, and configuration to be described, [visualizes] from the blue syllable *HŪṂ* situated upon the moon and sun in the lotus of his own heart, rays of the five wisdoms radiating forth. Having illuminated infinite world-systems, he summons the Blessed One together with his retinue, as well as the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas. Beholding them in the courtyard of the sky before him, he performs worship with offering substances arising from the *Gaganagañja-samādhi* from the seed-syllable in his own heart, through the hands of the Yoginīs—Mohavajrī and the others—seated within that maṇḍala-circle. He should then recite the seven verses of unsurpassed worship.

Then, the yogin himself—possessing the color, form, and shape that will be explained—visualizes at his own heart a blue syllable *hūṃ* resting upon a lotus, moon, and sun disk. From this, rays of light of the five wisdoms are emanated, illuminating the infinite world-systems, including the Blessed One together with his retinue.

Having also invited the gurus and bodhisattvas into the space before him, he gazes upon the assembly; then, after making offerings with the offering substances held in their hands—which have arisen from the seed-syllable at his own heart and from the Gaganagañja samādhi—the yoginīs, such as Mohavajrī and the others who abide in that circle, perform the worship.
Recite the verses for the seven unsurpassed offerings.
Whatever evil I have committed through both designation and intrinsic nature, and whatever evil I have rejoiced in— all that I confess.
In order to accumulate merit through the joy of the Perfectly Awakened One, his sons, and the Noble Ones,
I go for refuge to the Buddha, together with the Dharma and the Supreme Assembly.
Having established [the path], which resounds with the roar of the road,
and having especially surrendered your own bodies to you.
"I dedicate this merit that has been acquired toward perfect enlightenment;
having become the illustrious Caṇḍeśvara, I shall bring about the welfare of the world."
Whatever sinful deeds I have committed, both those that were proscribed and those that were natural, [I confess them all].
Whatever has been performed, I rejoice in it all; I confess all of that.
That Buddha and his noble sons rejoice in the accumulated merit.
I go for refuge to the Buddhas, together with the Dharma and the supreme Assembly.
I pray that you remain, proclaiming the melodic voice that teaches the Dharma of glorious beauty.
We shall offer our own bodies, especially so.
Whatever merit has been accumulated, that is dedicated toward perfect enlightenment.
Having become the glorious Lord Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, I shall bring benefit to sentient beings.

% ĀDIYOGA % = yoga, anuyoga, atiyoga % 2\verso Following that, having paid homage with body, speech, and mind and having offered praise to the Blessed One together with his retinue and attendants, one should dismiss them. Then, through wisdom characterized by the investigation of all phenomena, one should resolve that all phenomena are merely dependently originated, empty of intrinsic nature, equal to space, and of the very nature of the samādhi of union (yuganaddha). One should recite the mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*. Thus is yoga. || o ||

Then, having prostrated with deep devotion toward the body, speech, and mind of the Blessed One and his retinue, and having applied oneself with intense conviction in the nature of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one should recite the mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’haṃ*. This is the preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Then, in the infinite expanse of space, one should instantly visualize oneself as Vajrasattva—devoid of flesh, bone, blood, and so forth, resembling a mass of white light rays, great in tranquility, with two arms and one face, his lotus hands placed in the gesture of meditative equipoise (*samādhimudrā*), wearing a crown of matted locks, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and graced by the eighty minor signs, seated upon a white lotus and moon-disc on a sattva-cushion.
And it is said in the Tantra: "One should contemplate the body of the self as clear as a pure crystal. Thus ends the inquiry. ||o||

Then, from the center of the mandala of space, there appears the Great Peaceful Vajrasattva, who is devoid of his own flesh, bones, blood, and so forth, appearing like a mass of white light rays; he has one face and two hands, his lotus hands are in the mudrā of meditative concentration, he is adorned with a crown of matted locks, and he bears the thirty-two major marks.

One should visualize [the deity] adorned with the eighty minor marks, seated upon a lotus, a white lotus, and a moon disc in the sattvaparyaṅka posture. As it is also stated in the Tantra: "One should clearly meditate on one's own body as being like stainless, clear crystal. This is the subsequent yoga (anuyoga).

Then, having meditated upon a blue syllable *hūṃ* in the center of the union of sun and moon within the heart of oneself as Vajrasattva, and the thunderbolt marked with the syllable *hūṃ* produced from its transformation, as well as the lunar disc arising from that [thunderbolt] and all [the preceding elements] beginning with the sun; and having for a mere moment beheld the venerable Caṇḍeśvara—whose form is described below as exceedingly fierce—emerging from that [disc] before one, and then having re-absorbed him into oneself, one should become that very same fierce Caṇḍeśvara.

Then, having become firm in the nature of Vajrasattva, one should visualize at the heart, in the center of the union of a sun and moon disk, a blue syllable *hūṃ*. From the complete transformation of that, there arises a vajra marked with *hūṃ*. One should then contemplate all those [elements], such as the sun and so forth, as being the reflection of the moon.

Having visualized for a mere moment before oneself the glorious Caṇḍeśvara—who has emerged from that [source], who will be described later, and who possesses an extremely fierce form—one should again dissolve him back into oneself and meditate upon oneself as such a fierce Caṇḍeśvara, the most ferocious one.
And it is said in the Tantra: "One should visualize the Lord of the Mandala, arisen from the reflection of the sentient being."

It is also stated in the Tantra: "One should clearly visualize the maṇḍala of the sense faculties as arising from the reflection of the Hero (sattva). This is *CaMaTa* I.viii.9cd = *Saṃpuṭa* 3.3.10ab.

Then, embodying the aesthetic flavor of wrath (*krodharasa*), terrifying all the hosts of wicked obstructors (*vighna*) with his sword while loudly proclaiming: "HŪṂ 2 TRAṬ! Afflict them! HŪṂ 3 TRAṬ! Afflict them! BHO!", he binds them by the neck with the vajra-noose held in his left hand, and with the sword held in his right hand, saying "HŪṂ 2 PHAṬ 2," he should strike them until the hosts of obstructors raise cries of "Hā-hā!", some having their heads severed, some fleeing, and some dying.

Then, assuming an expression of wrath, he terrified the entire host of malevolent obstructors with his sword while uttering: *hūṃ hūṃ traṭ khedaya*, *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ traṭ khedaya bhoḥ*. Binding their throats with the vajra-noose held in his left hand, he [constrained them].

Holding a sword in his right hand, he uttered "hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ" and, like one intoxicated by music, let out the sound "hā hā" toward the hosts of obstructors; some [of the obstructors] were [consumed as] flesh.

Then, with a mind free from obstacles and full of joy, one should take the stake—which has a vajra-noose and blazing flames, and which is for the purpose of burning the island of fire—and, placing it upon the heads of the obstructors, strike it with the sword-born vajra-hammer. Reciting the piercing mantra from the top of the head down until it emerges from the anus-lotus, one should pierce them and cast them into the pit of the ten directions.

Then, with a mind free from obstacles and accompanied by joy, one should visualize the kīla—born from the blazing, intensely flaming, and incandescent Vajrapāśa—entering into a state of blazing upon the crowns of the obstructors. Striking it with the vajra-hammer arising from the sword, one should recite the kīla mantra as it emerges from the skull down to the secret lotus.
Having struck it with the ritual dagger (kīla), one should cause it to enter the well of the ten directions.

Then, in the east: Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa gha 2 ghātaya sarvaduṣṭendropendrān saparivārān kīlaya 2 hūṃ phaṭ! In the south: Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa gha 2 ghātaya sarvaduṣṭayamān saparivārān kīlaya 2 hūṃ phaṭ! In the west: Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa gha 2 ghātaya sarvaduṣṭavaruṇān saparivārān kīlaya 2 hūṃ phaṭ! In the north:

Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa gha 2! Slay all wicked Kuveras together with their retinues! Pin them down! Hūṃ Phaṭ! [In the southeast. Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa gha 2! Slay all wicked Agnis together with their retinues! Pin them down! Hūṃ Phaṭ! [In the southwest. Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa gha 2! Slay all wicked Nairṛtis together with their retinues! Pin them down! Hūṃ Phaṭ! [In the northwest. Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa gha 2! Slay all wicked Vāyus together with their retinues! Pin them down! Hūṃ Phaṭ!

[In the zenith: Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa gha 2! Slay all the wicked lords together with their retinues! Stake them! Hūṃ Phaṭ! [In the nadir: Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa gha 2! Slay all the wicked Brahmās together with their retinues! Stake them! Hūṃ Phaṭ! [In the nadir: Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa gha 2! Slay all the wicked Vemacitrins and earth-deities together with their retinues! Stake them! Hūṃ Phaṭ!

To the east: OṂ CAṆḌA MAHĀROṢAṆA GHA GHA GHĀTAYA SARVA DUṢṬĀN DRONDRAṆA SAPARIVĀRAṆA KĪLAYA KĪLAYA HŪṂ PHAṬ. To the south: OṂ CAṆḌA MAHĀROṢAṆA GHA GHA GHĀTAYA SARVA DUṢṬĀN MĀNASA SAPARIVĀRAṆA KĪLAYA KĪLAYA HŪṂ PHAṬ. To the west: OṂ CAṆḌA MAHĀROṢAṆA...

Gha gha ghātaya sarva-duṣṭān vāruṇān saṃparivāraṇān | kilaya kilaya hūṃ phaṭ | In the north: oṃ caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa | gha gha ghātaya sarva-duṣṭān kūberān saṃparivāraṇān | kilaya kilaya hūṃ phaṭ | On Mount Meru: oṃ caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa |

Gha gha ghātaya sarvaduṣṭāgnīn saṃparivāraṇa kīlaya kīlaya hūṃ phaṭ. In the southwest: oṃ caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa gha gha ghātaya sarvaduṣṭanairṛtīn saṃparivāraṇa kīlaya kīlaya hūṃ phaṭ. In the northwest: oṃ caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa gha gha ghātaya sarvaduṣṭavāyūn saṃparivāraṇa.

*Kīlaya kīlaya hūṃ phaṭ* | In the northeast: *oṃ caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa gha gha ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān saparivārān kīlaya kīlaya hūṃ phaṭ* | Above: *oṃ caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa gha gha ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān brahmāṇaḥ saparivārān kīlaya kīlaya hūṃ phaṭ* | Below:
oṃ caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa | gha gha ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān vaimatyikān pṛthivīdevatām saparivārām | kilaya kilaya hūṃ phaṭ ||

Thus, having understood that there is freedom from obstacles through the acts of piercing and striking, and having caused Caṇḍeśvara to disappear, one should again become the essence of Vajrasattva and meditate upon the mandalas of wind and so forth before oneself. Therein, one should meditate on [the seed-syllables] born from the syllable *yaṃ* and so forth, adorned with the syllable *laṃ*.

Having thus known that there are no obstacles because the kīla has been struck, he causes Caṇḍeśvara to vanish; then, in front of himself who has once again become the nature of Vajrasattva, he should visualize the maṇḍalas of wind and so forth. Among them, from the syllable YAṂ arises the wind maṇḍala, bow-shaped, dark blue, and marked with a banner.

Above that, from the syllable RAṂ, arises a red triangular fire maṇḍala marked at its corners with the syllable RAṂ. Above that, from the syllable BAṂ, arises a white circular water maṇḍala marked in its center with a vase. Above that, from the syllable LAṂ, arises a yellow square earth maṇḍala marked at its corners with three-pointed vajras.

Above that, one should visualize Mount Meru, composed of the four precious substances, arisen from the syllable *suṃ*; and upon that, in the center of a white source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*) pervading the expanse of space, a tiered vajra-palace arisen from a yellow *bhrūṃ*, which is dependently originated.

It has the nature of a condensed buddha-field that is utterly pure of mind-only; it is a great city of liberation, square with four gates, beautified by eight pillars, completely surrounded by four platforms, and adorned with four archways, as well as with jewel necklaces, half-necklaces, *vaktuli* ornaments, and arrow-head finials.
One should visualize it as being made exceedingly beautiful with melodic tones, and adorned with parasols, canopies, bells, fly-whisks, lions, and so forth, as well as banners fluttering in the wind.

Within his womb, upon a navel of a fully formed eight-petalled lotus, and above a moon and sun mandala that have arisen spontaneously, he beholds the Tathāgata Akṣobhya born from the syllable *HŪṂ*, embraced by Māmakī. Then those lords of yogins, having transferred [the seed] through the path of the immovable wheel of Akṣobhya, melt through the great passion of their love for Māmakī; together with the semen of Akṣobhya via the avadhūtī, they fall through the vajra-aperture into the interior of the goddess’s lotus, and enter within through the lotus-aperture.

Having empowered the right side of the womb with the seed-syllable *HŪṂ*, one should visualize oneself as the Lord of the Śrīcakra, emerging from lotuses in the form of the perfected Acala; then, through intense passion for Māmakī, having dissolved Akṣobhya within himself, he should behold himself as the Lord of the Śrīcakra, who has entered into union with Dveṣavajrī—the transformation of Māmakī—possessing the form, color, and configuration that will be described hereafter. This is the Atiyoga.

At its center, upon the seed-syllable *paṃ*, there arises an eight-petaled variegated lotus; at its pericarp, upon a moon disc arising from *āṃ* and a sun disc arising from *raṃ*, one visualizes the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, arisen from the syllable *hūṃ*, in perfect embrace with Māmakī.

Having descended from the path of the head of the Lord of Yogins Akṣobhya, he became enamored with Māmakī; through great passion, they melted, and the seminal essence of Akṣobhya fell from the vajra-aperture into the interior of the goddess’s lotus, entering within the opening of the lotus.

On the right side of the body, from the syllable *hūṃ* consecrated by the mantra, the form of Acala emerges perfectly manifested from a lotus; one should visualize that he, being intensely impassioned with Māmakī herself, dissolves into Akṣobhya. Then, [one should contemplate] the entry into union with Dveṣavajrī, who is the transformation of Māmakī, according to the forms and colors that will be explained.
One should view the embodied one as the very nature of the Guide of the glorious wheel; this is the supreme yoga.
Thus, the first samādhi, named Ādiyoga, consists of the threefold yoga. || o ||
NB: Yoga, Anuyoga, and Atiyoga = Ādiyoga = the first samādhi.
Thus, it is the first samādhi called "the initial application," which consists of the three yogas.

% MAṆḌALARĀJĀGRĪ % Then the yogin, whose nature is Acala, having emanated Prajñā in the form of Dveṣavajrī, [should place the syllables] for the sake of her family-circle (kulakalāpa): HŪṂ at her head, OṂ HŪṂ SVĀ ĀḤ HĀ on her navel, secret place, and pair of thighs, respectively.

Then, for the sake of generating the wisdom of the yogin, whose nature is immovable, in the form of Dveṣavajrī so as to consist of the five families, one should place OṂ, HŪṂ, SVĀ, ĀḤ, and HĀ respectively upon the crown of the head, the heart, the secret place, and the two thighs—[visualizing them] as a wheel, a vajra, a jewel, a lotus, and...

[One should] arrange the seed-syllables of the Tathāgatas upon the sword; then, upon the vajra and lotus produced from *hūṃ* and *āḥ*, [one should] visualize a yellow syllable *phaṭ* at the tip of the *āḥ* and *oṃ* produced from the *āḥ* and *oṃ*. Then, [one should visualize] the syllable *hrīḥ* located on the channels situated in the left and right limbs.

Having properly moved the index finger and the tongue, which are positioned at the tip [of the nose], preceded by the syllable *śī*, one should utter: *śīḥ śīḥ śīḥ oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajrasvabhāvātmako ’haṃ*, and thus begin the joy.

In order to generate the primordial wisdom of suchness through bliss, one should correctly illustrate how each respective stage arises. In that regard, there are kissing, embracing, and pressing the breasts.

Having held within the mouth of the wisdom-consort (prajñā) that mind characterized by the moments of arising joy—which arises from the mere union of the lotus and the vajra, such as the pressing of the fingers and so forth—one should correctly demonstrate it so that it is unwavering.

From the intense friction of the lotus and vajra, one should correctly manifest the mind characterized by the moment of the arising of supreme joy—which originates from the bodhicitta residing at the tip of the jewel—by holding it between the heart and the pair of breasts of the wisdom consort, pressing it exactly as it is, and making it motionless and firm like a life-force.

Having held within the womb of the portion of wisdom the mind— which is devoid of appearances of self and other, in which all activity has subsided, whose nature transcends speech and conceptualization, which is grounded solely in self-cognition, non-dual, and has the *dharmakāya* as its essence— one who perceives the stabilization of the breath in its prescribed immobility attains the three bodies more easily and more swiftly.

Perfectly generated from the bodhicitta placed upon the crest of the jewel, characterized by the moment of the arising of the coemergent, free from the appearance of self and other, transcending all agency, its nature being the complete suppression of verbal conceptualization, reaching the ultimate limit of singular self-awareness, and non-dual.

Having held the mind, which is the nature of the dharmakāya, within the bhaga of the Prajñā, one rests as it truly is; through the perfect indication of the motionless, vital breath, the three bodies—characterized by bliss and supreme bliss—are individually attained.

But when the *bodhicitta* falters, having become motionless, the mind characterized by the moment of the arising of the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*)—which consists of the mere sensation "I have experienced bliss"—should be observed as it remains steady. Then, through the application of the churning stick and the churning vessel, one should first create the White Mountain (*śvetācala*).

One should emanate yellow Acala in the east, red Acala behind [in the west], and dark-green Acala in the north; in the southeast, one should emanate Mohavajrikā of white luster; in the southwest, Piśunavajrī; in the northwest, the red Rāgavajrikā of golden hue; and in the northeast, one should emanate the dark-green Īrṣyāvajrikā. This is the second meditative absorption, named Maṇḍalarājāgrī. O ||

One should extract the green [syllable] from the mind characterized by the momentary arising of the joy of perfect awareness (*saṃvid*), which has the defining characteristic of the experience: "I have eaten with the bliss of the unwavering bodhicitta. [The goddess] Mohavajrā appears white in the southeast; Piśunavajrā, who is like gold, is in the southwest.
In the northwest, one should emanate red Rāgavajrī; in the northeast, one should emanate green Īrṣyāvajrī. This is the second meditative stabilization, called the Supreme King of Mandalas.

% Karmarājāgrī % Now, the Blessed One, permeated by great passion through the essence of the ultimate supreme great bliss (*atyantaparamamahāsukha*) together with his own consort (*svavidyā*), became established in the form of a seed-syllable (*bīja*) having attained the state of melting (*druta*). And it is said in the Tantra: "With consort, [he is] melted... — *Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa*.

Then, by means of the nectar of supreme great bliss that has utterly transcended existence, it melts into a drop (*bindu*) following after great passion together with self-awareness, and remains in the form of a seed-syllable. As it is also stated in the *Tantra*: "The melting begins together with wisdom."

Having observed that there was no lord, Māyāvajrī and the others were struck with wonder and became distressed, thinking, "We have become protectorless. To awaken their own minds, they invoked the Leader of the Mandala with vajra songs in verse: "O Pervasive Lord, having abandoned Maitreya..."

Do not make [all beings] empty by nature! Since I shall die if I am separated from you, do not make all wandering beings empty!—thus says Mūḍhāvajrī. Since I shall die if I am deprived of a compassionate mind, O Pervasive Lord, do not make them empty! Since this body of mine is afflicted by suffering, do not deprive it of life!—thus says Piśunavajrī. If you, O Wise One, are indeed...

Abandoning joy, enter into emptiness; my mind and all worlds without exception wait for you—thus says Rāgavajrī. Your eyes, though possessed of youth, are indifferent, empty, and fruitless; abandon this very nature of emptiness and apply yourself to equality with me—thus says Īrṣyāvajrī.
Having heard those words of distinction, they awoke as if from a dream; emerging from the form of their request, they emanated in the aspect of their own deities.

Having the appearance of a youth, possessing the form of fresh youthfulness, blue in color, with two arms and one face; his right hand brandishes a sword, while his left holds a yellow vajra-noose with the index finger at his heart; adorned with variegated garments and jewel ornaments; his crown marked with the letter *i*; having five locks of hair and a jeweled tiara; biting his lips, he tramples the four Māras; red-eyed and terrifying.

Furthermore, the Blessed One is situated in the center of a moon and sun mandala upon the hub of a multicolored lotus; he has a stooping posture, with his left knee planted on the ground and his right foot extended to the right. He possesses the form of fresh youth in the likeness of a sixteen-year-old, with a blue-colored body, one face, and two hands; his right hand brandishes a sword.

With his left hand, he holds a yellow vajra-noose together with a threatening gesture at his heart; he is clad in variegated garments and adorned with jewel ornaments. He wears a crown marked by the Lord of the Mind (Cittādhipati) and possesses five top-knots and a jeweled diadem. His teeth slightly overlap his lips, and with eyes that gaze askance and are red, he strikes terror [into beings] while completely conquering the four Māras.

His Prajñā, Dveṣavajrī, is blue in color, with a pair of arms adorned with a curved knife and a skull-cup; she is decorated with variegated garments and jewel ornaments, and is intent on impassioning the Blessed One.

*Asya prajñā dveṣavajrī nīlā kartikapālānvitabhujayugmā vicitravastraratnābharaṇamaṇḍitā bhagavantam anurāgayantī.* Her Prajñā, Dveṣavajrī, is blue in color, possessing a pair of arms beautified by a curved knife and a skull-cup; she is adorned with variegated garments and jewel ornaments, and is striving to impassion the Blessed One.
However, all the heroes beginning with Śvetācala should be meditated upon as being like Cakreśvara; [the heroines] beginning with Mohavajrī should be visualized as equal to Dveṣavajrī.

All the heroes (vīra), such as Acala, Akṣobhya, and so forth, should be meditated upon as being like Cakreśvara; and all the heroines (vīrā), such as Mohavajrī and so forth, should be meditated upon as being like Dveṣavajrī.

Thus, having seen the mandala circle fully perfected all around, pervading the expanse of the sky with a mass of light rays, one should generate the sense of "I" within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*). In the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is Vairocana; in the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is Vajrasūrya; in the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is Padmanarteśvara; in the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is Vajrarāja; in the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is Vajrasattva. In the eyes is Mohavajrī; in the ears is Dveṣavajrī; in the nostrils is Īrṣyāvajrī; in the mouth is Rāgavajrī; in touch is Piśunavajrī. The earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is Pātanī; the water element (*ab-dhātu*) is Māra-... [the text here is incomplete].

Having visualized the expanse of space pervaded by the mass of light rays from the thus-perfected wheel of the maṇḍala, one should cultivate the divine pride (*ahaṃkāra*) regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields. One should regard the aggregate of form as Vairocana; the aggregate of feeling as Vajrasūrya; and the aggregate of perception as Padmanarteśvara.

In the aggregate of formations is Vajrarāja; in the aggregate of consciousness is Vajrasattva. In the two eyes is Mohavajrī; in the two ears is Dveṣavajrī; in the two nostrils is Īrṣyāvajrī; in the mouth is Rāgavajrī; in touch is Piśunavajrī. The earth element is Pātanī; the water element is Māraṇī.
The earth element is Ākarṣaṇī; the wind element is Padmanarteśvarī; and the space element is Padmajālinī.

At the crown of the head, the throat, and the heart, [one recites] *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*. Then, with the light rays from the seed-syllable at one’s own heart, one summons the wisdom maṇḍala before oneself; and with the mantra beginning *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ*, one banishes all obstructors.

Having presented the water for the face, the water for the feet, and so forth, and having made offerings and praises, one recites three times: *oṃ śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇa saparivāra sahita ākarṣaya ākarṣaya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ ātma-maṇḍale adhiṣṭhānaṃ kuru hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Through this, the wisdom of the summoning and other rites [is invoked].

Having perfected the identity of oneself as the samayasattva and cultivated the divine pride, one requests the five Tathāgatas—summoned into the sky by light rays from the heart of the deity who possesses divine pride—together with the hosts of heroes and heroines, saying: "I pray that all the Tathāgatas confer empowerment upon me."

One should visualize those Tathāgatas holding jewel victory vases in their hands, as it is said in the passage beginning, "Just as at the moment of birth," and so forth, conferring empowerment upon oneself. While the empowerment is being conferred, a great divine festival will arise.
Dzo dzo dzdzo ta! The Vajra Consort bathes the Victors; the wrathful deities proceed to the ten directions with their own bodies.
From the center of the sky, a rain of sandalwood, saffron, and other fragrant substances, along with supreme flowers and precious jewels, [falls].
The sons of the Jinas, together with their retinues, being exceedingly joyful and satisfied, [are characterized by] hymns of praise and auspiciousness.
The bodies of the Lord of Munis are adorned with the jewels of qualities and extend infinitely in all directions through their infinite elements.
Accompanied by melodious songs, praises, and auspicious verses, the assembly of the Sons of the Victorious Ones celebrates with joy and festive delight.
The precious ornaments of the qualities of the Muni’s body pervade all the infinite and vast realms.

When that [consecration] is present, the Blessed One is sealed by the mind; by that very [sealing], the Wrathful Vajrīs are white and so forth, and the Delusion Vajrīs and so forth are [sealed] by Śāśvata, Ratneśa, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi. Then, having ripened the entire realm of sentient beings with rays from the seed-syllable in the heart and established them in the abode of Acala, one should withdraw those rays again, visualize them within the seed-syllable, and then resolve that the entire triple world is the interior of the maṇḍala-circle.

From the initiation, [the disciples] are sealed by the Lord through the Power of Mind (*cittādhipati*), and by that very [power], they are [sealed] by Dveṣavajrī. [They are also sealed] by the heroes such as white Acala and the consorts such as Mohavajrī, and by Ratneśa, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi.

Then, one should meditate that the light rays from the seed-syllable at the heart bring all realms of sentient beings without exception to full maturity, establishing them in the state of immovability; thereafter, those light rays are withdrawn and dissolved back into the seed-syllable. Then, one should visualize the entirety of the three realms as the form of the mandala circle.

The Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśvara), too, through his intense passion for the beautiful body of Mohavajrī, first internalizes Śvetācala within himself by way of the Vajrācala-path; then, having himself become Śvetācala and likewise withdrawing [the visualization], he enters into union with Dveṣavajrī, becomes Śrī-Kṛṣṇācala, and should cultivate the ego-identification: "I alone am the accomplished one (siddha) who is immovable."
The Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśvara), through his passion for the supreme limb of Mohavajrī, first enters via the path of his own crown as the white Acala; he himself then becomes the white Acala.

In that very way, having condensed [the deities], one should enter into meditative union with Mohavajrā, who is the transformation of Vajrā. Likewise, having condensed oneself through the respective sequences of yellow Acalā and the others, one enters into meditative union with each of the yoginīs, such as Piśunavajrā and the rest.
Thereafter, having entered into meditative union with Dveṣavajrī and become the glorious black Acala, one should cultivate the pride, thinking, "I myself am the accomplished Acala."

And it is said in the Tantra: "Having impassioned the four goddesses, the ascetic should withdraw the entire maṇḍala; he should meditate intensely upon himself as the single *saṃpuṭa*. Thus ends the third meditative absorption, named Karmarājāgra. ||o||

It is also stated in the *Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa-tantra*: "Through passion for the four goddesses, one should perfectly gather all mandalas; the practitioner of the vow should intensely meditate upon them as a single union with oneself. This is the third samādhi, called the Supreme King of Action.

% SŪKṢMAYOGAḤ % Thus, having visualized the entire threefold realm as the single body whose nature consists of wisdom and means, one should recite the mantra according to the samaya. *Oṃ caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hūṃ phaṭ*— this is the root mantra.

oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūḥ candrarūpa | catta catta | pratta pratta | kaha kaha | prasphara prasphara | prasphāraya prasphāraya | hana hana | grasa grasa | bandha bandha | jambhaya jambhaya | stambhaya stambhaya | mohaya mohaya | sarvaśatruṃ nāṃ mukhabandhanaṃ kuru kuru.

*Sarva-dākinīnāṃ graha-bhūta-piśāca-vyādhi-yakṣāṇām | trāsaya trāsaya | mara mara | māraya māraya | ruru caṇḍa ruru rakṣa rakṣa | caṇḍa mahā-sena | sarva-mahā-sena | sarva-mājñāpaya yati | oṃ caṇḍa mahā-roṣaṇa hūṃ phaṭ |* This is the mantra of the garland; it is the recitation of the mantra.

Then, Dveṣavajrī, together with the curved knife (*kartṛ*), entered the seed-syllable at the heart of the Blessed One and emerged as an emanated wheel; blazing and with the tips of fierce heat (*caṇḍālī*), she [united] with the Tathāgatas together with their vidyās who resided upon their respective wheels within that emanated wheel.

Having burned the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*) abiding in the *saṃbhogakāya* mandala, as well as the syllable *ha* abiding in the *mahāsukha* mandala, one should visualize the indestructible bodhicitta marked with a sword being held within the seed-syllable at the heart.

Having placed a drop (*bindu*) upon the moon as the indication of the *dharmadhātu*, thereupon all phenomena became of a single flavor—devoid of permanence, annihilation, and the middle, and established merely as the sound of bliss that is non-abiding everywhere. Thus is the subtle yoga.

That seed-syllable, which is the nature of the five Buddhas, should be visualized as blazing. Furthermore, the syllable *huṃ* is the nature of envy (*īrṣyā*); the syllable *āḥ* is passion (*rāga*); the syllable *ha* is slander (*paiśunya*); the syllable *re* is malice (*pārūṣya*); *kha* is delusion (*moha*), which is merged with the half-moon; the half-moon is hatred (*dveṣa*), which is merged with the bindu; and the bindu is dissolved into the *nāda* of the dharmadhātu.

Then, one should abide in the great bliss that is the nature of the single taste of all phenomena, free from permanence, nihilism, and a middle, and not abiding in anything at all; this is the subtle yoga.

Furthermore, by the power of his previous vows and in accordance with the dispositions of the beings to be trained (*vaineya-sattva*), the yogin—becoming as immovable as a mountain—should behold the Lord of the Mandala together with his retinue suddenly manifested in the form of the mandala-circle, and then commence the reality of the offering (*bali-tattva*).

Furthermore, having visualized the Lord of the Mandala together with his retinue as arising in the form of the mandala-circle, accomplished through the power of previous aspirations and the influence of the dispositions of the sentient beings to be trained, one who practices the yoga that is like [the state of] Acala should begin the reality of the *bali* offering.

Having placed before oneself vessels and so forth arising from the syllable *khaṃ*, filled with special foods, enjoyments, and the like, [one visualizes] upon a wind mandala arising from *yaṃ* the fire arising from *raṃ*, [upon which is] *oṃ āḥ*.

Upon a three-legged stand in the form of a human head arising from *hūṃ*, there is a white lotus vessel filled with the syllable *āḥ*. Within it, all manner of food and so forth—arising from *bhrūṃ āṃ jrīṃ khāṃ hūṃ lāṃ māṃ pāṃ tāṃ bāṃ*—are established in the form of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*).

Blessed by those seeds, they blaze with the force of the fire mandala; scorched by that blazing, they melt and take on the appearance of the sun. Above that, one visualizes a sword of the nature of nectar, one cubit in length, arising from the syllable *hūṃ* at the tip of its handle. One should contemplate that it melts and blends through the heat [of the fire], becoming cool like quicksilver.

Upon that, one should summon the wisdom nectar of the heroes and heroines dwelling in the ten directions through the light rays of the three *tattvas*, and having caused it to enter into that very [place], visualize the syllable *oṃ* and the others also gradually melting; then, consecrate it with the three *tattvas*.

oṃ namo bhagavate śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇāya devāsura-manuṣyatrāsanāya kālamārāvalavināśanāya ratnamukuṭakṛtaśirase | ehi baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa mama sarvavighnān hara hara caturmārānnivāraya nivāraya | trāsa trāsa | bhrāma bhrāma | tsthiṃda tsthiṃda ||

*bhiṃ da bhiṃ da | na śā | śātāpatāpa śoṣa śoṣa | tstshe da tstshe da | bhe da bhe da duṣṭasattvān mā vighna kuru citta kaṃbha śmī kuru kuru hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.* With this mantra, one should offer the *bali* (food offering) to the Blessed One together with his retinue.

Then, having been drawn in through the hollow of the light rays from the *hūṃ* vajra-tongue of the Blessed One and his retinue, [the offerings] were consumed and [the deities] were seen to be delighted. Having satisfied them with the mantra beginning with *oṃ āḥ khāro mukhaṃ*, and having offered the rinsing of the mouth and so forth, they were worshipped and praised.

Having requested forbearance by reciting the hundred-syllable mantra, one should request [the deities] to depart; this is the ritual for the torma offering. Thus, having realized that the entire threefold world is the nature of the maṇḍala circle—like the moon in water—and through the yoga that does not obstruct any of the sense faculties and does not abide in anything, one should dwell in whatever way is comfortable.

Furthermore: Knowing reality as the immovable self, the yogi wanders everywhere like a lion with no fixed abode, just as it is. Disrespectful toward the pure and harsh toward worldly beings, appearing unmoving like the nature of phenomena, he knows the reality of unborn dharmas and becomes one who enjoys compassion. Here, he is one who harms those who injure the Teaching.

One brings an end to the malevolent; having seized their substances, one acts for the benefit of sentient beings. Therefore, one should never falsely conceal the faults of oneself or others. Likewise, one should observe the commitments (*samaya*) of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). One should not distinguish between what is edible and what is inedible, nor should one avoid what is traversable and what is untraversable.

One should neither perform what is to be done nor what is not to be done; one should abandon both the drinkable and the undrinkable. Upon the head is a crest-jewel, and upon the ears are earrings. On the feet are anklets, and likewise a girdle around the waist. Furthermore, the glorious Lord Acala is adorned with various jewels; he holds a sword in his right hand and grasps a noose with his left.

Having cast [the skull] away, one should fashion a curved knife (kartṛkā) from it and adorn it with jewels. One should accomplish the state of being unmoved by the bliss of the twenty-year-old Wisdom Consort. Having accomplished the consumption of food, feasts, and so forth, consecrated by the three realities, one should dwell roaming like a lion, bowing the head before the Guru, the chosen deity, and others.

"Entering into meditative equipoise in luminosity, one should proceed while remaining in samādhi. Aroused by the exhortations of songs, one awakens perfectly. Through the application of secret conduct, one who is of a non-conceptual nature will achieve accomplishment. Thus it is said.
Or, having resorted [to them] under the power of ignorance;
This treatise has arisen from the fault of forgetfulness.
Whatever has been done therein, [to that] glorious Vajra...
O hosts of ḍākinīs, may you all grant me your forbearance.
Through the forest jewel of one who strives in restraint, there arises here the realization of immovability.
The faultless foundation was first requested by Sarvamitra.
Even when urged by others, the noble ones perform what is well-done; by that, they remain supreme and unshakable.
May the six superknowledges arise in this very life!
The *Abhisamaya* of Immovability, titled "The Joyful," is hereby completed.

This was composed in the presence of the master Śrī Vanaratna. At the center of the southern land, the one of great intelligence known as Śrī Amoghavajrasiddhi requested [this work] from the venerable Ānandasādhu, a great follower of the tradition of the glorious Samantabhadra’s forest hermitage who is fully versed in all the profound and vast systems of tenets.

This was translated by the monk Zhönnu Pal, a proponent of the Dharma who possesses knowledge of the well-composed branches [of learning], following the command of His Holiness himself, together with a generous gift of tea.
